g.text: A. What goes in and what comes out
Sample task: room 1, "Send the red ball over the gray barrier so that it comes down and hits the blue ball within one and a half seconds, without touching the barrier."
Scene graph (the manifest): one row per object, 27 rows
each row = 3 ids + 76 numbers: flags 8 | pose 9 | velocity 6 | geometry 21 | physical 14 | support 9 | container 6 | provenance 3
The red ball row, as the network receives it
flags dynamic 1 sphere 1 box 0 mesh 0 front axis 0
geometry visual box -0.10..0.10 m on each axis
physical log mass log(0.2 kg) friction 0.90 restitution 0.00
support none -> 9 zeros container none -> 6 zeros

g.text: x1 - x0 is the true direction from the
w = 1.0 for objects that move in the truth
w = 0.1 for objects that stay still
From the denoised estimate x1_hat = x_tau + (1 - tau) u_hat, each
frame's position change must match the average velocity: p_t - p_(t-1) =
dt (v_(t-1) + v_t) / 2, outside contact frames. This is the evaluator's
own check, so the model trains on the rule it is scored by.
For each movable object: which object does it touch first, and when? The
floor and whatever it rests on do not count. Sample truth here: red ball
-> blue ball at 0.87 s. This is exactly what the benchmark's forecast
The predicted collision boxes of two objects must not overlap in any
frame. A stand-in for the evaluator's 5 mm penetration probe, which
needs PhysX and cannot run inside a training step.
Prediction: start from a noise sample x0 and take 32 small steps along u_hat to reach x1, which decodes to the 60 frames (well under a second on one
GPU). Variant A, the deterministic regressor: the same network with no noise and a fixed tau, one pass, loss (x1_hat - x1)^2; it is the control the
flow model must beat on grazing contacts.

g.text: pose(t+1) = pose(t) + change, velocities replaced. The new
state becomes the next input: 60 passes from the post-launch
state, then frames[] is written as in the other variants.
Any state along the way can be edited and the rollout

path.style: fill: none; stroke: #4d4d4d; stroke-width: 1.8; stroke-linecap: round

g.text: Every stored PhysX transition (state t -> state t+1) is one example, so the 60 transitions of a trajectory
train in parallel. Loss: squared error on the normalised change, objects that stay still weighted 0.1; the
kinematic-consistency term carries over, and the first-contact head becomes "who touches whom in the next
At rollout time the model sees its own slightly wrong states, which it never saw in training. Remedies: (1)
add small noise to the input state during training so the model learns to pull a drifted state back; (2)
unroll 8 steps during training and apply the loss to all of them; (3) optional per-step flow head that
samples the change instead of regressing it, for grazing contacts.
Joint model (B): one sampling run for all 60 frames, pair geometry from frame 0 only, no error pile-up, fixed horizon. Step model (D): 60 passes, pair geometry
recomputed every step so contacts are always current, errors pile up, any horizon, edit the state at any step. Diffusion Forcing sits between them: one network, a
separate noise level per frame, frames denoised in order.
C. Where the simulator is used, and where it is not
Random launches and drops in procedural rooms,
rolled out in PhysX and stored as trajectories.
Today 47 s per rollout: a fresh Isaac world,
3,840 physics steps, a contact read every step.
Plan: one world per scene, reset in place

path.style: fill: none; stroke: #4d4d4d; stroke-width: 1.8; stroke-linecap: round

g.text: Every training step compares the network's
output with a stored trajectory. Nothing is
simulated; a step costs about one second on one
GPU for a batch of 64 trajectories.

flow model: well under a second per scene. This
is what would stand in for the simulator.

g.text: The frozen evaluator replays the same launch in
PhysX, probes contacts at the predicted poses
and checks the goal. One rollout per benchmark
The 47 seconds per PhysX rollout are paid in step 1, once per training trajectory, and in step 4, once per benchmark task. Training steps and predictions never call the simulator. Red boxes
use PhysX; blue boxes are the learned model alone.
